From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a complete **List of National Historic Landmarks in Utah**. The United States [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Utah#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The state of [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah") is home to 14 of these landmarks, tying together a wide range of historic threads.

The table below lists all 14 of these sites, along with added detail and description.

As [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Church_(LDS_Church) "President of the Church (LDS Church)") of [the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints") at the time of the [Mormon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mormon "Mormon") settlement of the [Salt Lake Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_Valley "Salt Lake Valley"), Young and his home were pivotal in the development of the Church, [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah"), and the [American west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States"). |

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a complete **List of National Historic Landmarks in Utah**. The United States [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Utah#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The state of [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah") is home to 14 of these landmarks, tying together a wide range of historic threads.

The table below lists all 14 of these sites, along with added detail and description.

As [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Church_(LDS_Church) "President of the Church (LDS Church)") of [the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints") at the time of the [Mormon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mormon "Mormon") settlement of the [Salt Lake Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_Valley "Salt Lake Valley"), Young and his home were pivotal in the development of the Church, [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah"), and the [American west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States"). |

## Determining the Eligibility of a Property for National Historic Landmark Designation

This page will help you determine whether your property may be eligible for nomination as an NHL.  
  
 In simple terms, your property must:

*   be of national significance under one or more of the six NHL criteria
*   retain a high degree of integrity.

## National Significance

Nationally significant properties tell important stories that have meaning for all Americans, regardless of where they live.

A nationally significant property may:

*   Be the location of an event that had a significant impact on American history overall. 
*   Be the property most strongly associated with a nationally significant figure in American history.
*   Provide an outstanding illustration of a broad theme or trend in American history overall.
*   Be an outstanding example of an architectural style or significant development in engineering.
*   Be part of a group of resources that together form a historic district.
*   Be a property that can provide nationally significant archeological information. 

There are a few **exceptions** to bear in mind:

*   Not every property owned by the federal government or associated with a federal program is nationally significant and eligible to be an NHL.
*   Not every property associated with a national event or person is eligible to be an NHL.
*   Not every property representing an outstanding architectural style, engineering feat, work of a master architect, or work of a significant engineer is eligible to be an NHL.
*   Not every property with archeological information potential is eligible to be an NHL.

NHL Program staff members will assist you in determining whether a property is nationally significant.

## High Degree of Integrity

Integrity is the ability of a property to convey its historical associations or attributes. While the NHL and National Register of Historic Places (NR) programs use the same [seven aspects of historical integrity](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm) to evaluate properties – location, setting, design, materials, workmanship, feeling, and association – NHLs must retain them to a higher degree than required for NR listing. If the resource has been more than modestly modified or has deteriorated since its [period of national significance](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm), it may meet the NR threshold for integrity, but not the higher NHL standard.

A property with a nationally significant association may qualify for NHL designation only if it also retains, to a high degree, the physical features that made up its historic character and appearance.  
  
 The integrity requirement for an archeological property differs; visit the [glossary](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm) to learn more about archeological integrity.

## Six Criteria for National Significance

The NHL program uses six criteria to assess the national significance of properties nominated as NHLs. These criteria are codified in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The full listing of the criteria can be found in [36 CFR § 65](http://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?c=ecfr&SID=ba70f95b53b8134ac1a8fe78c4ebe118&tpl=/ecfrbrowse/Title36/36cfr65_main_02.tpl).

**Please note:** While you may use more than one criterion for a nomination, using one criterion is usually sufficient. Nominations that use multiple criteria are not stronger or better nominations than those which use only one criterion.

### Criterion 1

> _**Properties that are associated with events that have made a significant contribution to,**_**_and are identified with, or that outstandingly represent, the broad national patterns of United States history and from which an understanding and appreciation of those patterns may be gained._**

This criterion is used for properties that are associated with major events or major patterns in American history. The property should possess one of the strongest associations possible with a nationally significant historical event or pattern.

Nominations using Criterion 1 must also include a discussion of comparable properties associated with this major historic event or pattern. This discussion should clarify why the nominated property possesses the strongest association with a specific event or pattern over the other associated properties.

*   **Criterion 1 Example (event):**[Edmund Pettus Bridge](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710530), Selma, AL
*   **Criterion 1 Example (trend):**[Colorado Fuel and Iron Company Administrative Complex](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713726), Pueblo, CO

### Criterion 2

> _**Properties that are associated importantly with the lives of persons nationally significant in the history of the United States.**_

This criterion is used for properties associated with individuals who have made a significant or exceptional contribution to American history. The individual's association with the property must be connected to the specific period when he or she made his or her contributions to American history. Properties that are not associated with an individual's significant accomplishments, such as birthplaces, childhood homes, vacation homes, or retirement homes, are usually not eligible.

Properties using Criterion 2 must be compared to other similar properties to identify the one that possesses the strongest association with a person's contributions. The length of residency is often an important factor when assessing similar properties.

*   **Criterion 2 Example:**[Klagetoh (Leegito) Chapter House](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713725), Klagetoh, AZ

### Criterion 3

> _**Properties that represent some great idea or ideal of the American people.**_

This criterion relates to properties that represent an overarching ideal that is foundational to the United States. NHLs designated under this criterion are associated with endeavors or goals of the highest order such as attaining democracy, achieving freedom, and securing fundamental rights. The application of this criterion requires the most careful scrutiny and _applies only in rare instances_.

A property eligible for NHL designation under Criterion 3 will also be eligible under Criterion 1 or 2, and eligibility for NHL designation is primarily evaluated under Criterion 1 or 2.

*   **Criterion 3 Example:**[Carter G. Woodson Home (Updated Documentation)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/702401), Washington, DC

### Criterion 4

> _**Properties that embody the distinguishing characteristics of an architectural type specimen exceptionally valuable for a study of a period, style, or method of construction,or that represent a significant, distinctive and exceptional entity whose components may lack individual distinction.**_

This criterion is used for properties that are exceptionally important works for their design, either as an individual building or a collection of buildings/resources comprising a district.

The property might be a key work of a nationally significant architect or builder. Not all works of a documented master are eligible for NHL designation. For example, while all of Frank Lloyd Wright's extant buildings may be nationally significant given his importance, only those that represent his career benchmarks and/or designs that have become iconic within his body of work may be eligible for designation.

A property can also be considered under Criterion 4 as one of the best examples of an important type, period, form, or construction method (such as its engineering). It cannot be merely a competent design or representative example. The importance of a property type is determined by prevailing scholarship. Artistic value is considered only in the context of history's judgment in order to avoid conflicts with current taste and aesthetic trends.

*   **Criterion 4 Example:**[Samara (John E. and Catherine E. Christian House](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/711160)), West Lafayette, IN

### Criterion 5

> _**Properties that are composed of integral parts of the environment not sufficiently significant by reason of historical association or artistic merit to warrant individual recognition but collectively compose an entity of exceptional historical or artistic significance, or outstandingly commemorate or illustrate a way of life or culture.**_

This criterion covers groups of resources known as [historic districts](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm). Most of the individual resources within historic districts could not stand alone as National Historic Landmarks; however, collectively they are associated with a nationally significant event, movement, or broad pattern of national development.

A majority of the historic districts that are recognized by this criterion are nationally significant for their extraordinary historic importance in illustrating or commemorating a way of life or culture or for their potential to reveal important information. Criterion 5 is rarely used on its own; many of these historic districts also use Criterion 1 or 6.

**Please note** that this criterion is rarely used for historic districts that are nationally significant for their architectural significance under Criterion 4.

*   **Criterion 5 Example:**[Chicano Park](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710320), San Diego, CA (Criteria 1 and 5)
*   **Criterion 5 Example:**[Lower Pecos Canyonlands Archeological District (redacted)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713944), Val Verde County, TX (Criteria 5 and 6)

### Criterion 6

> _**Properties that have yielded or may be likely to yield information of major scientific importance by revealing new cultures, or by shedding light upon periods of occupation over large areas of the United States. Such sites are those which have yielded, or which may reasonably be expected to yield, data affecting theories, concepts and ideas to a major degree.**_

This criterion most often recognizes nationally significant archeological properties. Data produced at these sites have already produced and are likely to yield nationally significant information.

Use of this criterion requires a discussion of how recoverable data are likely to substantially modify a major historic concept, resolve a substantial historical or anthropological debate, or close a serious gap in a major theme of American history. These arguments are generally made by discussing specific, nationally significant research questions which may be answered by the data contained in the property. Research questions can be related to property-specific issues, to broader questions about a large geographic area, or to theoretical issues independent of any particular geographic location.

*   **Criterion 6 Example:**[Hueco Tanks (redacted)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713928), El Paso, TX

## Special Consideration - NHL Exceptions 1-8

Properties which fall into the following categories require special consideration in order to be designated as NHLs. If a property is eligible for an exception, it generally has to meet higher standards in its other criteria for designation. If your property fits into any of these categories, please check with your NHL reviewer to see if it may still be eligible for NHL designation. The examples below are NHLs which were designated with an exception in each one of these categories:

**Exception 1:** Properties owned by religious institutions or used for religious purposes either historically or currently.

**Examples:**[First Presbyterian Church](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710733)**,**Stamford, CT; and[Tolson's Chapel and School](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710517)**,**Sharpsburg, MD

**Exception 2:** Buildings or structures that have been moved from their original historic location. Exception 2 is most frequently used to justify contributing status of moved buildings within a district.

**Examples: Depot (pp. 14, 40),**[Western Railroad Stone Arch Bridges and Chester Factory Village Depot](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710641)**,**Becket, Middlefield, and Chester, MA; and[Hamilton Grange (2016 update)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710735)**,**New York, NY

**Exception 3:** Site of a building or structure no longer standing.

**Example:**[Central Utah Relocation Center (Topaz)](https://catalog.archives.gov/id/72000733)**,**Millard County, UT

**Exception 4:** Birthplaces and graves of historical figures.

**Example:**[Wyandotte National Burying Ground (Eliza Burton Conley Burial Site)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/711415),Kansas City, KS

**Exception 5:** Cemeteries.

**Example:**[Green-Wood Cemetery](https://catalog.archives.gov/id/75315781)**,**Brooklyn, NY

**Exception 6:** Reconstructed buildings or grouping of buildings.

**Example:**[Zoar Historic District](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710778)**,**Zoar, OH

**Exception 7:** Properties that are primarily commemorative in nature.

**Example:**[Ames Monument](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710317)**,**Albany County, WY

**Exception 8:** Properties that have achieved national significance within the past 50 years.

**Example:**[May 4, 1970, Kent State Shootings Site](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710742)**,**Kent, OH

#### Checklist - Eligibility

1. Can I provide evidence that my property is nationally significant?

2. Which of the NHL criteria does my property address?

3. Does my property require an exception and, if so, have I consulted with NHL staff about it?

## Determining the Eligibility of a Property for National Historic Landmark Designation

This page will help you determine whether your property may be eligible for nomination as an NHL.  
  
 In simple terms, your property must:

*   be of national significance under one or more of the six NHL criteria
*   retain a high degree of integrity.

## National Significance

Nationally significant properties tell important stories that have meaning for all Americans, regardless of where they live.

A nationally significant property may:

*   Be the location of an event that had a significant impact on American history overall. 
*   Be the property most strongly associated with a nationally significant figure in American history.
*   Provide an outstanding illustration of a broad theme or trend in American history overall.
*   Be an outstanding example of an architectural style or significant development in engineering.
*   Be part of a group of resources that together form a historic district.
*   Be a property that can provide nationally significant archeological information. 

There are a few **exceptions** to bear in mind:

*   Not every property owned by the federal government or associated with a federal program is nationally significant and eligible to be an NHL.
*   Not every property associated with a national event or person is eligible to be an NHL.
*   Not every property representing an outstanding architectural style, engineering feat, work of a master architect, or work of a significant engineer is eligible to be an NHL.
*   Not every property with archeological information potential is eligible to be an NHL.

NHL Program staff members will assist you in determining whether a property is nationally significant.

## High Degree of Integrity

Integrity is the ability of a property to convey its historical associations or attributes. While the NHL and National Register of Historic Places (NR) programs use the same [seven aspects of historical integrity](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm) to evaluate properties – location, setting, design, materials, workmanship, feeling, and association – NHLs must retain them to a higher degree than required for NR listing. If the resource has been more than modestly modified or has deteriorated since its [period of national significance](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm), it may meet the NR threshold for integrity, but not the higher NHL standard.

A property with a nationally significant association may qualify for NHL designation only if it also retains, to a high degree, the physical features that made up its historic character and appearance.  
  
 The integrity requirement for an archeological property differs; visit the [glossary](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm) to learn more about archeological integrity.

## Six Criteria for National Significance

The NHL program uses six criteria to assess the national significance of properties nominated as NHLs. These criteria are codified in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The full listing of the criteria can be found in [36 CFR § 65](http://www.ecfr.gov/cgi-bin/text-idx?c=ecfr&SID=ba70f95b53b8134ac1a8fe78c4ebe118&tpl=/ecfrbrowse/Title36/36cfr65_main_02.tpl).

**Please note:** While you may use more than one criterion for a nomination, using one criterion is usually sufficient. Nominations that use multiple criteria are not stronger or better nominations than those which use only one criterion.

### Criterion 1

> _**Properties that are associated with events that have made a significant contribution to,**_**_and are identified with, or that outstandingly represent, the broad national patterns of United States history and from which an understanding and appreciation of those patterns may be gained._**

This criterion is used for properties that are associated with major events or major patterns in American history. The property should possess one of the strongest associations possible with a nationally significant historical event or pattern.

Nominations using Criterion 1 must also include a discussion of comparable properties associated with this major historic event or pattern. This discussion should clarify why the nominated property possesses the strongest association with a specific event or pattern over the other associated properties.

*   **Criterion 1 Example (event):**[Edmund Pettus Bridge](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710530), Selma, AL
*   **Criterion 1 Example (trend):**[Colorado Fuel and Iron Company Administrative Complex](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713726), Pueblo, CO

### Criterion 2

> _**Properties that are associated importantly with the lives of persons nationally significant in the history of the United States.**_

This criterion is used for properties associated with individuals who have made a significant or exceptional contribution to American history. The individual's association with the property must be connected to the specific period when he or she made his or her contributions to American history. Properties that are not associated with an individual's significant accomplishments, such as birthplaces, childhood homes, vacation homes, or retirement homes, are usually not eligible.

Properties using Criterion 2 must be compared to other similar properties to identify the one that possesses the strongest association with a person's contributions. The length of residency is often an important factor when assessing similar properties.

*   **Criterion 2 Example:**[Klagetoh (Leegito) Chapter House](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713725), Klagetoh, AZ

### Criterion 3

> _**Properties that represent some great idea or ideal of the American people.**_

This criterion relates to properties that represent an overarching ideal that is foundational to the United States. NHLs designated under this criterion are associated with endeavors or goals of the highest order such as attaining democracy, achieving freedom, and securing fundamental rights. The application of this criterion requires the most careful scrutiny and _applies only in rare instances_.

A property eligible for NHL designation under Criterion 3 will also be eligible under Criterion 1 or 2, and eligibility for NHL designation is primarily evaluated under Criterion 1 or 2.

*   **Criterion 3 Example:**[Carter G. Woodson Home (Updated Documentation)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/702401), Washington, DC

### Criterion 4

> _**Properties that embody the distinguishing characteristics of an architectural type specimen exceptionally valuable for a study of a period, style, or method of construction,or that represent a significant, distinctive and exceptional entity whose components may lack individual distinction.**_

This criterion is used for properties that are exceptionally important works for their design, either as an individual building or a collection of buildings/resources comprising a district.

The property might be a key work of a nationally significant architect or builder. Not all works of a documented master are eligible for NHL designation. For example, while all of Frank Lloyd Wright's extant buildings may be nationally significant given his importance, only those that represent his career benchmarks and/or designs that have become iconic within his body of work may be eligible for designation.

A property can also be considered under Criterion 4 as one of the best examples of an important type, period, form, or construction method (such as its engineering). It cannot be merely a competent design or representative example. The importance of a property type is determined by prevailing scholarship. Artistic value is considered only in the context of history's judgment in order to avoid conflicts with current taste and aesthetic trends.

*   **Criterion 4 Example:**[Samara (John E. and Catherine E. Christian House](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/711160)), West Lafayette, IN

### Criterion 5

> _**Properties that are composed of integral parts of the environment not sufficiently significant by reason of historical association or artistic merit to warrant individual recognition but collectively compose an entity of exceptional historical or artistic significance, or outstandingly commemorate or illustrate a way of life or culture.**_

This criterion covers groups of resources known as [historic districts](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalhistoriclandmarks/glossary.htm). Most of the individual resources within historic districts could not stand alone as National Historic Landmarks; however, collectively they are associated with a nationally significant event, movement, or broad pattern of national development.

A majority of the historic districts that are recognized by this criterion are nationally significant for their extraordinary historic importance in illustrating or commemorating a way of life or culture or for their potential to reveal important information. Criterion 5 is rarely used on its own; many of these historic districts also use Criterion 1 or 6.

**Please note** that this criterion is rarely used for historic districts that are nationally significant for their architectural significance under Criterion 4.

*   **Criterion 5 Example:**[Chicano Park](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710320), San Diego, CA (Criteria 1 and 5)
*   **Criterion 5 Example:**[Lower Pecos Canyonlands Archeological District (redacted)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713944), Val Verde County, TX (Criteria 5 and 6)

### Criterion 6

> _**Properties that have yielded or may be likely to yield information of major scientific importance by revealing new cultures, or by shedding light upon periods of occupation over large areas of the United States. Such sites are those which have yielded, or which may reasonably be expected to yield, data affecting theories, concepts and ideas to a major degree.**_

This criterion most often recognizes nationally significant archeological properties. Data produced at these sites have already produced and are likely to yield nationally significant information.

Use of this criterion requires a discussion of how recoverable data are likely to substantially modify a major historic concept, resolve a substantial historical or anthropological debate, or close a serious gap in a major theme of American history. These arguments are generally made by discussing specific, nationally significant research questions which may be answered by the data contained in the property. Research questions can be related to property-specific issues, to broader questions about a large geographic area, or to theoretical issues independent of any particular geographic location.

*   **Criterion 6 Example:**[Hueco Tanks (redacted)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/713928), El Paso, TX

## Special Consideration - NHL Exceptions 1-8

Properties which fall into the following categories require special consideration in order to be designated as NHLs. If a property is eligible for an exception, it generally has to meet higher standards in its other criteria for designation. If your property fits into any of these categories, please check with your NHL reviewer to see if it may still be eligible for NHL designation. The examples below are NHLs which were designated with an exception in each one of these categories:

**Exception 1:** Properties owned by religious institutions or used for religious purposes either historically or currently.

**Examples:**[First Presbyterian Church](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710733)**,**Stamford, CT; and[Tolson's Chapel and School](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710517)**,**Sharpsburg, MD

**Exception 2:** Buildings or structures that have been moved from their original historic location. Exception 2 is most frequently used to justify contributing status of moved buildings within a district.

**Examples: Depot (pp. 14, 40),**[Western Railroad Stone Arch Bridges and Chester Factory Village Depot](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710641)**,**Becket, Middlefield, and Chester, MA; and[Hamilton Grange (2016 update)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710735)**,**New York, NY

**Exception 3:** Site of a building or structure no longer standing.

**Example:**[Central Utah Relocation Center (Topaz)](https://catalog.archives.gov/id/72000733)**,**Millard County, UT

**Exception 4:** Birthplaces and graves of historical figures.

**Example:**[Wyandotte National Burying Ground (Eliza Burton Conley Burial Site)](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/711415),Kansas City, KS

**Exception 5:** Cemeteries.

**Example:**[Green-Wood Cemetery](https://catalog.archives.gov/id/75315781)**,**Brooklyn, NY

**Exception 6:** Reconstructed buildings or grouping of buildings.

**Example:**[Zoar Historic District](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710778)**,**Zoar, OH

**Exception 7:** Properties that are primarily commemorative in nature.

**Example:**[Ames Monument](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710317)**,**Albany County, WY

**Exception 8:** Properties that have achieved national significance within the past 50 years.

**Example:**[May 4, 1970, Kent State Shootings Site](https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/DownloadFile/710742)**,**Kent, OH

#### Checklist - Eligibility

1. Can I provide evidence that my property is nationally significant?

2. Which of the NHL criteria does my property address?

3. Does my property require an exception and, if so, have I consulted with NHL staff about it?

Kansas National Historic Landmarks (clickable map)

This is a list of all [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmarks "National Historic Landmarks") designated by the U.S. government in [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"). There are 26 National Historic Landmarks (NHLs) in Kansas.

The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Kansas#cite_note-NHLQA-1)

The [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas") is home to 26 of these landmarks, illustrating the state's [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_United_States "Military of the United States") and [frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier "Frontier") heritage, as well as its contributions to the broader themes of the [Civil Rights Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement"), the [Progressive Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism"), and others.

Kansas National Historic Landmarks (clickable map)

This is a list of all [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmarks "National Historic Landmarks") designated by the U.S. government in [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"). There are 26 National Historic Landmarks (NHLs) in Kansas.

The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Kansas#cite_note-NHLQA-1)

The [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas") is home to 26 of these landmarks, illustrating the state's [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_United_States "Military of the United States") and [frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier "Frontier") heritage, as well as its contributions to the broader themes of the [Civil Rights Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement"), the [Progressive Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism"), and others.

The **List of National Historic Landmarks in Montana** contains the landmarks designated by the [U.S. Federal Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Federal_Government "U.S. Federal Government") for the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). There are 28 [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") (NHLs) in Montana.

The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources [nationwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of U.S. National Historic Landmarks by state") according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Montana#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The Montana landmarks emphasize its frontier heritage, the passage of the [Lewis and Clark Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_and_Clark_Expedition "Lewis and Clark Expedition"), Montana's contributions to the [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park "National park") movement, and other themes.

Three sites in Montana extend across the [Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho "Idaho") or [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") state line, and are listed by the National Park Service as [Idaho NHLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Idaho "List of National Historic Landmarks in Idaho") or [North Dakota NHLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_North_Dakota "List of National Historic Landmarks in North Dakota").

The **List of National Historic Landmarks in Montana** contains the landmarks designated by the [U.S. Federal Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Federal_Government "U.S. Federal Government") for the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"). There are 28 [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") (NHLs) in Montana.

The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")[National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources [nationwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of U.S. National Historic Landmarks by state") according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Montana#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The Montana landmarks emphasize its frontier heritage, the passage of the [Lewis and Clark Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_and_Clark_Expedition "Lewis and Clark Expedition"), Montana's contributions to the [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park "National park") movement, and other themes.

Three sites in Montana extend across the [Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho "Idaho") or [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") state line, and are listed by the National Park Service as [Idaho NHLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Idaho "List of National Historic Landmarks in Idaho") or [North Dakota NHLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_North_Dakota "List of National Historic Landmarks in North Dakota").

There are 29 National Historic Landmarks in Colorado, two of which extend into [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Colorado#cite_note-NHLlist-1)

This is a list of [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") in [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"). There are 29 National Historic Landmarks in Colorado, two of which extend into [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Colorado#cite_note-NHLlist-1)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/GAUDENS_O.jpg/250px-GAUDENS_O.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GAUDENS_O.jpg)

The studio of [Augustus Saint-Gaudens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Saint-Gaudens "Augustus Saint-Gaudens") in [Cornish, NH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish,_New_Hampshire "Cornish, New Hampshire"). The [Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gaudens_National_Historical_Park "Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park") is New Hampshire's only unit of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service").

New Hampshire currently has 24 National Historic Landmarks; the most recent addition was [Lucknow (Castle in the Clouds)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_in_the_Clouds "Castle in the Clouds") in [Moultonborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moultonborough,_New_Hampshire "Moultonborough, New Hampshire") added in 2024.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_Hampshire#cite_note-1) Three of the sites—[Canterbury Shaker Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Shaker_Village "Canterbury Shaker Village"), [Harrisville Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrisville_Historic_District_(Harrisville,_New_Hampshire) "Harrisville Historic District (Harrisville, New Hampshire)"), and the [MacDowell Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacDowell_Colony "MacDowell Colony")—are categorized as [National Historic Landmark Districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark_District "National Historic Landmark District"). One site, the [Augustus Saint-Gaudens Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gaudens_National_Historical_Park "Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park"), is categorized as a [National Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historical_Park "National Historical Park").

The [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated in the United States under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources [nationwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of U.S. National Historic Landmarks by state") according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_Hampshire#cite_note-NHLQA-2) National Historic Landmarks are a subset of the properties listed in the larger [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").

## Related state and federal historic sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_Hampshire&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Related state and federal historic sites")]

Of the state's National Historic Landmarks, the National Park Service operates only one, the [Augustus Saint-Gaudens Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gaudens_National_Historical_Park "Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park"). The state operates some of them as historic sites:

*   [Franklin Pierce Homestead Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce_Homestead "Franklin Pierce Homestead")
*   [Robert Frost Farm Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Frost_Farm_(Derry,_New_Hampshire) "Robert Frost Farm (Derry, New Hampshire)")
*   [Wentworth-Coolidge Mansion Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wentworth-Coolidge_Mansion "Wentworth-Coolidge Mansion")

The state also operates the [Daniel Webster Birthplace State Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster_Birthplace_State_Historic_Site "Daniel Webster Birthplace State Historic Site"), which is not far from the [Daniel Webster Family Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster_Family_Home "Daniel Webster Family Home") listed above.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/GAUDENS_O.jpg/250px-GAUDENS_O.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GAUDENS_O.jpg)

The studio of [Augustus Saint-Gaudens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Saint-Gaudens "Augustus Saint-Gaudens") in [Cornish, NH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish,_New_Hampshire "Cornish, New Hampshire"). The [Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gaudens_National_Historical_Park "Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park") is New Hampshire's only unit of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service").

New Hampshire currently has 24 National Historic Landmarks; the most recent addition was [Lucknow (Castle in the Clouds)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_in_the_Clouds "Castle in the Clouds") in [Moultonborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moultonborough,_New_Hampshire "Moultonborough, New Hampshire") added in 2024.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_Hampshire#cite_note-1) Three of the sites—[Canterbury Shaker Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Shaker_Village "Canterbury Shaker Village"), [Harrisville Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrisville_Historic_District_(Harrisville,_New_Hampshire) "Harrisville Historic District (Harrisville, New Hampshire)"), and the [MacDowell Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacDowell_Colony "MacDowell Colony")—are categorized as [National Historic Landmark Districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark_District "National Historic Landmark District"). One site, the [Augustus Saint-Gaudens Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gaudens_National_Historical_Park "Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park"), is categorized as a [National Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historical_Park "National Historical Park").

The [National Historic Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") program is operated in the United States under the auspices of the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), and recognizes structures, districts, objects, and similar resources [nationwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of U.S. National Historic Landmarks by state") according to a list of criteria of national significance.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_Hampshire#cite_note-NHLQA-2) National Historic Landmarks are a subset of the properties listed in the larger [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").

## Related state and federal historic sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_Hampshire&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Related state and federal historic sites")]

Of the state's National Historic Landmarks, the National Park Service operates only one, the [Augustus Saint-Gaudens Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Gaudens_National_Historical_Park "Saint-Gaudens National Historical Park"). The state operates some of them as historic sites:

*   [Franklin Pierce Homestead Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce_Homestead "Franklin Pierce Homestead")
*   [Robert Frost Farm Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Frost_Farm_(Derry,_New_Hampshire) "Robert Frost Farm (Derry, New Hampshire)")
*   [Wentworth-Coolidge Mansion Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wentworth-Coolidge_Mansion "Wentworth-Coolidge Mansion")

The state also operates the [Daniel Webster Birthplace State Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster_Birthplace_State_Historic_Site "Daniel Webster Birthplace State Historic Site"), which is not far from the [Daniel Webster Family Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster_Family_Home "Daniel Webster Family Home") listed above.

Illinois National Historic Landmarks (clickable map)

This list of [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmarks "National Historic Landmarks") in [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), has 89 entries including [Eads Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eads_Bridge "Eads Bridge"), which spans into [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and which the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service") credits to [Missouri's National Historic Landmark list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Missouri "List of National Historic Landmarks in Missouri"). Also added are two sites that were once National Historic Landmarks before having their designations removed. All National Historic Landmarks of the United States are also listed on the more general, [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").

The National Historic Landmark Program is administered by the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), a branch of the [Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior"). The National Park Service determines which properties meet NHL criteria and makes nomination recommendations after an owner notification process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The [Secretary of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior") reviews nominations and, based on a set of predetermined criteria, makes a decision on NHL designation or a determination of eligibility for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-Title36-2) Both public and privately owned properties can be designated as NHLs. This designation provides indirect, partial protection of the historic integrity of the properties via tax incentives, grants, monitoring of threats, and other means.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-NHLQA-1) Owners may object to the nomination of the property as an NHL. When this is the case the Secretary of the Interior can only designate a site as eligible for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-Title36-2)

Illinois National Historic Landmarks (clickable map)

This list of [National Historic Landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmarks "National Historic Landmarks") in [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), has 89 entries including [Eads Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eads_Bridge "Eads Bridge"), which spans into [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and which the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service") credits to [Missouri's National Historic Landmark list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Missouri "List of National Historic Landmarks in Missouri"). Also added are two sites that were once National Historic Landmarks before having their designations removed. All National Historic Landmarks of the United States are also listed on the more general, [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").

The National Historic Landmark Program is administered by the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service"), a branch of the [Department of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Interior "United States Department of the Interior"). The National Park Service determines which properties meet NHL criteria and makes nomination recommendations after an owner notification process.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-NHLQA-1) The [Secretary of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior") reviews nominations and, based on a set of predetermined criteria, makes a decision on NHL designation or a determination of eligibility for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-Title36-2) Both public and privately owned properties can be designated as NHLs. This designation provides indirect, partial protection of the historic integrity of the properties via tax incentives, grants, monitoring of threats, and other means.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-NHLQA-1) Owners may object to the nomination of the property as an NHL. When this is the case the Secretary of the Interior can only designate a site as eligible for designation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Illinois#cite_note-Title36-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Designation by the US government

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/In_the_18th_century%2C_Independence_Hall_was_known_as_the_Pennsylvania_State_House._The_building_housed_all_three_branches_of_the_%287f78b5f4-6a05-4885-af23-89c28d3631cd%29.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:In_the_18th_century,_Independence_Hall_was_known_as_the_Pennsylvania_State_House._The_building_housed_all_three_branches_of_the_(7f78b5f4-6a05-4885-af23-89c28d3631cd).jpg)

[Independence National Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_National_Historical_Park "Independence National Historical Park") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), one of the nation's most visited National Historic Landmark Districts

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Navajo_Nation_Council_Chamber%2C_January_2019.jpg/250px-Navajo_Nation_Council_Chamber%2C_January_2019.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Navajo_Nation_Council_Chamber,_January_2019.jpg)

The [Navajo Nation Council Chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navajo_Nation_Council_Chamber "Navajo Nation Council Chamber"), the seat of government for [Navajo Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navajo_Nation "Navajo Nation") in [Window Rock, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Window_Rock,_Arizona "Window Rock, Arizona"), was declared a National Historic Landmark in 2004.

A **National Historic Landmark** (**NHL**) is a [building, district, object, site, or structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places_property_types "National Register of Historic Places property types") that is officially recognized by the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") for its outstanding historical significance. Only some 2,500, or roughly three percent, of over 90,000 places listed on the country's [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") (NRHP) are recognized as National Historic Landmarks.

A [National Historic Landmark District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark_District "National Historic Landmark District") may include many [contributing properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contributing_properties "Contributing properties") that are buildings, structures, sites or objects, and it may also include non-contributing properties. Contributing properties may or may not also be separately listed as NHLs or on the NRHP.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Historic_Landmark&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Historic_Landmark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 19th century")]

The origins of the first National Historic Landmark was a simple cedar post, placed by the [Lewis and Clark Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_and_Clark_Expedition "Lewis and Clark Expedition") on their 1804 outbound trek to the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") in commemoration of the death from natural causes of Sergeant [Charles Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Floyd_(explorer) "Charles Floyd (explorer)"). The cedar plank was later replaced by a 100 ft (30 m) marble obelisk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-1) The [Sergeant Floyd Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergeant_Floyd_Monument "Sergeant Floyd Monument") in [Sioux City, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux_City,_Iowa "Sioux City, Iowa"), was officially designated on June 30, 1960.

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Historic_Landmark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 20th century")]

Prior to 1935, efforts to preserve [cultural heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_heritage "Cultural heritage") of national importance were made by piecemeal efforts of the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress"). In 1935, Congress passed the [Historic Sites Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_Sites_Act "Historic Sites Act"), which authorized the [interior secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior") authority to formally record and organize historic properties, and to designate properties as having "national historical significance", and gave the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service") authority to administer historically significant federally owned properties.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-2) Over the following decades, surveys such as the [Historic American Buildings Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_American_Buildings_Survey "Historic American Buildings Survey") amassed information about culturally and architecturally significant properties in a program known as the Historic Sites Survey.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-3)

Most of the [designations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designation_(heritage_assets) "Designation (heritage assets)") made under this legislation became [National Historic Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Sites_(United_States) "National Historic Sites (United States)"), although the first designation, made December 20, 1935, was for a [National Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Memorials_of_the_United_States "List of National Memorials of the United States"), the [Gateway Arch National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateway_Arch_National_Park "Gateway Arch National Park"), then known as the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial, in [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), Missouri. The first National Historic Site designation was made for the [Salem Maritime National Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salem_Maritime_National_Historic_Site "Salem Maritime National Historic Site") on March 17, 1938.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-4)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Tucson05_TitanICBM.jpg/250px-Tucson05_TitanICBM.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tucson05_TitanICBM.jpg)

The [Titan Missile Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_Missile_Museum "Titan Missile Museum") in [Tucson, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucson,_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona"), a National Historic Landmark

In 1960, the [National Park Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Park_Service "National Park Service") began administering the survey data gathered under this legislation, and the National Historic Landmark program began to take more formal shape.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-5) When the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") was established in 1966, the National Historic Landmark program was encompassed within it, and rules and procedures for inclusion and designation were formalized. Because listings (either on the National Register, or as an NHL) often triggered local preservation laws, legislation in 1980 amended the listing procedures to require owner agreement to the designations.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-6)

On October 9, 1960, 92 places, properties, or districts were announced as eligible to be designated NHLs by [U.S. Secretary of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Interior "United States Secretary of the Interior")[Fred A. Seaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_A._Seaton "Fred A. Seaton"). Agreements of owners or responsible parties were subsequently obtained, but all 92 have since been considered listed on that 1960 date.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-7)

## Criteria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Historic_Landmark&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Criteria")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Global_Citizen_Festival_Central_Park_New_York_City_from_NYonAir_%2815351915006%29.jpg/250px-Global_Citizen_Festival_Central_Park_New_York_City_from_NYonAir_%2815351915006%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Global_Citizen_Festival_Central_Park_New_York_City_from_NYonAir_(15351915006).jpg)

[Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), a prominent National Historic Landmark; New York City has [116 NHLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_York_City "List of National Historic Landmarks in New York City"), more than any other city in the U.S.

NHLs are designated by the United States secretary of the interior because they are:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-9)

*   Sites where events of national historical significance occurred;
*   Places where prominent persons lived or worked;
*   Icons of ideals that shaped the nation;
*   Outstanding examples of design or construction;
*   Places characterizing a way of life; or
*   Archeological sites able to yield information.

## Current National Historic Landmarks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Historic_Landmark&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Current National Historic Landmarks")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Museo_del_Antiguo_Legado_Estadounidense%2C_T%C3%A1nger%2C_Marruecos%2C_2015-12-11%2C_DD_44-46_HDR.JPG/250px-Museo_del_Antiguo_Legado_Estadounidense%2C_T%C3%A1nger%2C_Marruecos%2C_2015-12-11%2C_DD_44-46_HDR.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museo_del_Antiguo_Legado_Estadounidense,_T%C3%A1nger,_Marruecos,_2015-12-11,_DD_44-46_HDR.JPG)

The [American Legation in Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Legation,_Tangier "American Legation, Tangier") in [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco"), the first National Historic Landmark on foreign soil

[More than 2,500 NHLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_by_state "List of National Historic Landmarks by state") have been designated. Most, but not all, are in the United States. There are NHLs in all 50 states and the national capital of [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Three states ([Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Pennsylvania "List of National Historic Landmarks in Pennsylvania"), [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Massachusetts "List of National Historic Landmarks in Massachusetts"), and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_York "List of National Historic Landmarks in New York")) account for nearly 25 percent of the nation's NHLs. Each of three cities within these states, [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Philadelphia "List of National Historic Landmarks in Philadelphia"), [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Boston "List of National Historic Landmarks in Boston"), and [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_New_York_City "List of National Historic Landmarks in New York City"), has by itself more NHLs than 40 of the 50 states. New York City alone has more NHLs than all but five states: [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Virginia "List of National Historic Landmarks in Virginia"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_California "List of National Historic Landmarks in California"), Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and New York, the latter of which has the most NHLs of all 50 states. There are 74 NHLs in the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Washington,_D.C. "List of National Historic Landmarks in Washington, D.C.").

Some NHLs are in [U.S. commonwealths and territories, associated states, and foreign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_United_States_commonwealths_and_territories,_associated_states,_and_foreign_states "List of United States National Historic Landmarks in United States commonwealths and territories, associated states, and foreign states"). There are 15 in [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), the [Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Islands "Virgin Islands"), and other [U.S. commonwealths and territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_(U.S._state) "Commonwealth (U.S. state)"); five in U.S.-associated states such as [Micronesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federated_States_of_Micronesia "Federated States of Micronesia"); and [one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Legation,_Tangier "American Legation, Tangier") in [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-NHL_list-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-11)

[Over 100 ships or shipwrecks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._National_Historic_Landmark_ships_and_shipwrecks "List of U.S. National Historic Landmark ships and shipwrecks") have been designated as NHLs.

Approximately half of the National Historic Landmarks are [privately owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property "Property").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-12) The National Historic Landmarks Program relies on suggestions for new designations from the National Park Service, which also assists in maintaining the [landmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmarks "Landmarks"). A friends' group of owners and managers, the National Historic Landmark Stewards Association, works to preserve, protect and promote National Historic Landmarks.

If not already listed on the National Register of Historic Places, an NHL is automatically added to the Register upon designation; about three percent of Register listings are NHLs. [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_National_Historic_Landmarks_in_Washington,_D.C. "List of National Historic Landmarks in Washington, D.C.") is home to three specifically legislated exceptions to this rule: the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), the [United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol"), and the [United States Supreme Court Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court_Building "United States Supreme Court Building"). All are designated as NHLs, but are not on the National Register.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark#cite_note-13)
